findings.title: ES384 and ES512 tests use a 256-bit EC key and do not verify the re-encoded DER signature
findings.body: `ECDSAAlgorithmTest` generates a single default `EC` key pair (256-bit `secp256r1`) in the constructor and reuses it for `ES256`, `ES384`, and `ES512`. Because ECDSA signature components `r` and `s` are bounded by the key's curve order rather than the hash size, signing with a 256-bit key always produces ~32-byte `r` and `s` values (~70-byte DER signatures) even when using `SHA384withECDSA` and `SHA512withECDSA`. As a result, `testES512` never produces a DER sequence longer than 127 bytes, leaving the multi-byte DER length encoding and decoding paths (`length > 127` in `ASN1Encoder.writeLength` and `ASN1Decoder.readLength`) untested. In addition, `test()` only asserts that `asn1Des` decodes back to `rsConcat2` without verifying `asn1Des` against `Signature.verify(asn1Des)` (or `Assert.assertArrayEquals(sign, asn1Des)`), so a broken DER encoding that round-trips through `ASN1Decoder` would not be caught. Each algorithm should be tested with its matching curve (`secp256r1`, `secp384r1`, `secp521r1`) and the re-encoded DER signature should be verified with `Signature.verify`.

findings.title: Unused ASN1Encoder.create().write(...) calls in concatenatedRSToASN1DER
findings.body: In `concatenatedRSToASN1DER`, lines 114-115 call `ASN1Encoder.create().write(rBigInteger)` and `ASN1Encoder.create().write(sBigInteger)` and discard the returned encoders before performing the exact same encoding again inside `writeDerSeq(...)` on lines 119-120. Lines 114-115 are dead code that perform unnecessary allocations and encoding on every signature conversion.
